title: Ecology: Levels of Organisation and Associations Between Organisms
summary: The meaning of ecology, biotic and abiotic factors, the levels from individual to biosphere, and the five kinds of association between living things.

p: Ecology is the scientific study of the relationships between living things and their surroundings. The word comes from the Greek oikos ('house') and logos ('study'): it is the study of the 'house' in which living things live.

Think of an ecosystem as a neighbourhood. Each organism has a job (its niche), deals with its neighbours (biotic factors, the living things such as plants, animals and microbes) and with the physical surroundings (abiotic factors, the non-living things such as rainfall, temperature, light, soil, pH and wind).
From the smallest to the largest:

Individual: one organism, for example one lion. Population: all the individuals of one species in one area, for example the pride of lions in Yankari Game Reserve. Community: all the populations of different species living and interacting in an area (lions, zebras, grasses, trees and bacteria). Ecosystem: the community together with its non-living environment (soil, rain, sunlight). Biome: a very large region with a similar climate and similar plants and animals, for example the tropical savanna or the tropical rainforest. Biosphere: all the parts of Earth where life exists, from the deepest ocean to the high mountains.
No organism lives completely alone. Species form close, long-term relationships, called associations or symbiosis. The signs + (benefits), – (harmed) and 0 (not affected) are used to show who gains.

p: Strictly, scientists use 'symbiosis' for close living-together such as mutualism, commensalism and parasitism. Predation and competition are interactions but not always called symbiosis. Also, the lesson note says 'the tree is neither harmed nor helped' by the orchid; in a few cases a heavy load of epiphytes may harm a tree, but we treat the standard case as commensalism.
The Serengeti example in many books is in Tanzania. In Nigeria you can use Yankari, Gashaka-Gumti or Okomu National Park instead.

title: Tolerance and Adaptation
summary: Shelford's law of tolerance, the zones of the tolerance curve, and the structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations of organisms.

p: Tolerance is the ability of an organism to live and reproduce within a certain range of an environmental factor, such as temperature, pH or salt concentration. Shelford's law says that each organism has a minimum, an optimum and a maximum for each factor, and it cannot survive outside this range.

img.alt: A bell-shaped curve showing the zones of intolerance, physiological stress and optimum for an organism

p: Optimum range (the middle of the curve): the factor is at its best level, so the population is largest, healthiest and breeds well.
Zones of physiological stress (on both sides): the factor is too low or too high. The organism lives but is weak, grows slowly and cannot breed well.
Zones of intolerance (the far ends): the organism cannot live and soon dies.

Example: the fish tilapia has a temperature range. If the pond becomes too cold or too hot, the fish move into stress zones and die if they cannot escape. Different species have different ranges; a species with a wide range (such as the rat) is widespread, while one with a narrow range (such as some corals) is easily harmed by change.
An adaptation is an inherited feature that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment. There are three kinds.

Structural adaptations are body features. Cactus (xerophyte): spines (leaves reduced to cut water loss), thick fleshy stem that stores water, deep or wide roots. Fish: streamlined body to reduce drag, gills to take oxygen from water, fins for steering. Camel: hump stores fat, long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out sand, broad pads do not sink in sand.

Physiological adaptations are internal processes. Cactus (CAM photosynthesis): opens stomata at night to take in CO₂ and so loses less water in the hot day. Bears in cold lands hibernate (slow their body activity) to save energy. Salt-water fish pass out the extra salt through their gills and make little urine. Nigerian example: the lungfish aestivates in the mud during the dry season.

Behavioural adaptations are actions. Wildebeest migrate to areas with fresh grass and water. Desert animals are nocturnal (active at night) to avoid the heat. Birds make nests and weaver birds build hanging nests to avoid snakes.

title: Pollution: Air and Water
summary: The meaning of pollution, and the causes, effects and control of air pollution (including acid rain) and water pollution (including eutrophication).

p: Pollution is the introduction of harmful substances (pollutants) into the environment, causing harm to living things or to the environment itself. A pollutant is any substance in the wrong place, in the wrong amount, or at the wrong time.

Causes: factory fumes (sulphur dioxide SO₂ and oxides of nitrogen NOx); smoke and carbon monoxide from vehicles, generators and power plants; bush burning; dust from quarrying and cement factories; gas flaring in oil-producing areas; aerosol sprays (CFCs).

Effects: breathing diseases such as asthma, bronchitis and lung cancer; carbon monoxide (CO) joins with haemoglobin and prevents it from carrying oxygen (this is why using a generator in a closed room can kill); acid rain, in which SO₂ and NOx dissolve in rain to form acids that damage buildings (zinc roofs corrode), kill fish and harm crops and forests; global warming and climate change caused by greenhouse gases such as CO₂ and methane; and damage to the ozone layer by CFCs.

Control: use cleaner energy (solar, wind, hydro, natural gas); fit catalytic converters in vehicles and filters on factory chimneys; make and enforce laws about emissions; plant trees (afforestation); stop bush burning and gas flaring.

img.alt: A diagram showing how sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from factories and vehicles form acid rain that falls on forests, lakes and buildings
img.cap: How acid rain forms and what it harms.

p: Causes: untreated sewage and household waste; factory waste (effluent) containing metals and chemicals; run-off from farms carrying fertiliser and pesticides; oil spills from tankers and pipelines (a serious problem in the Niger Delta); dumping of refuse in drains and rivers.

Effects: eutrophication; water-borne diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery; poisoning and death of fish and other water life; oil on the water surface cuts oxygen and light, and coats the feathers of water birds; heavy metals such as mercury build up in food chains and harm people who eat the fish.

Control: build and maintain sewage treatment plants; treat factory effluent before release; make laws against dumping and punish offenders; educate the public; use fertiliser in the right amounts; clean up oil spills with booms, skimmers and bacteria that eat oil.

1. Fertiliser or sewage, rich in nitrates and phosphates, enters a river or lake. 2. Algae grow very fast and cover the surface (an algal bloom). 3. The algae block the light, so the plants below die. 4. Bacteria decompose the dead algae and plants and use up the dissolved oxygen. 5. Fish and other animals suffocate and die. 6. The water becomes smelly and unfit to drink.

img.alt: A flow chart of eutrophication from fertiliser run-off to algal bloom, oxygen loss and death of fish

title: Pollution: Soil and Noise, and the Control of Pollution
summary: The causes, effects and control of land pollution and noise pollution, with a summary table of all four types.

p: Causes: dumping of domestic and industrial solid waste, especially non-biodegradable materials such as plastics, polythene bags and sachet-water bags; too much fertiliser and pesticide; mining and quarrying; oil spills and chemical waste; electronic waste (e-waste).

Effects: the soil loses fertility and crop yield falls; poisons seep through the soil into underground water (leaching); soil organisms such as earthworms and useful bacteria die; flooding, because refuse blocks drains; breeding places for flies, mosquitoes and rats which spread diseases.

Control: the 3 R's: Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again) and Recycle (turn waste into new things); use biodegradable products; bioremediation (using bacteria and fungi to clean polluted soil); organic farming; proper waste disposal and sanitary landfill; planting cover crops.
Noise is unwanted loud sound, measured in decibels (dB). Sound above about 85 dB over a long time can damage hearing.
Causes: traffic and horns, factories, generators, aircraft, loudspeakers at markets, churches, mosques and parties.
Effects: hearing loss; stress, headache and high blood pressure; poor sleep and poor concentration; it disturbs communication of animals and may drive them away.
Control: plant trees as sound barriers; use silencers on engines and generators; fit soundproof materials in buildings; keep factories away from homes; make and enforce laws about noise levels.
Study the table.

Do not litter, do not burn rubbish in the open, sort waste, use sachet-water bags only once and recycle them, service your generator, and write to local government about problems in your community. Good laws only work when people obey them.

title: Conservation of Natural Resources
summary: Conservation versus preservation, and the methods of conserving soil, water, forests and wildlife.

p: Conservation is the wise and sustainable use and management of natural resources so that they are not wasted, destroyed or made extinct, and are available for future generations.

Conservation is not the same as preservation. In conservation resources are used wisely (for example, selective felling, where only mature trees are cut). In preservation, nature is protected from any use at all (for example, a strict nature reserve where people cannot enter).

Importance: soil grows our food, filters water and supports many living things. Erosion by rain and wind removes the fertile top layer (a big problem in the south-east of Nigeria with gully erosion, and desert encroachment in the north).

Methods: contour ploughing (ploughing across the slope, not up and down, to slow run-off); terracing steep slopes; crop rotation (changing crops each season to keep nutrients); cover crops such as beans or sweet potato; mulching (covering the soil with dead leaves); planting trees and grass as windbreaks and shelter belts; adding manure; avoiding over-grazing.
Importance: water is needed for all life, for farming and for industry.

Methods: drip irrigation (water goes straight to the roots); rainwater harvesting; building dams and reservoirs; repairing leaking pipes; protecting river banks and wetlands; not wasting water; treating and reusing waste water.
Importance: forests give timber, firewood, food and medicine; they take in CO₂ and give out oxygen; they control climate and rainfall; they stop erosion and floods; and they shelter many species.

Methods: afforestation (planting trees where there were none) and reforestation (replanting where trees were cut); selective felling instead of clear-felling; forest reserves and national parks; laws against illegal logging; use of gas, kerosene or solar energy instead of firewood and charcoal; tree-planting campaigns.
Importance: keeps biodiversity and the balance of nature, gives food and medicine, supports tourism and has scientific and beauty value.

Methods: game reserves and national parks (for example Yankari, Kainji Lake, Cross River National Park and Okomu); laws against poaching (illegal hunting) and trade in animal products such as ivory and pangolin scales; captive breeding of endangered species (for example in zoos) to release later; education and community involvement; controlling hunting seasons.

title: Pests of Crops
summary: The kinds of crop pests (chewing, piercing and sucking, boring, nematodes, birds and rodents), the damage they do and the effects of pests on production.

p: A pest is any organism that harms crops, livestock or people or causes economic loss. Most crop pests are insects.

img.alt: A chart of common crop pests such as caterpillars, grasshoppers, aphids, weevils and rodents

p: Biting and chewing insects have strong jaws (mandibles) that cut leaves, stems and fruits. Examples: grasshoppers, locusts, beetles, caterpillars, fall armyworm. Damage: notched or eaten leaves (defoliation), holes in fruits.

Piercing and sucking insects have needle-like mouthparts (stylets) that pierce the plant and suck sap. Examples: aphids, mealybugs, whiteflies, leafhoppers, cotton stainers. Damage: yellow leaves (chlorosis), wilting, stunted growth, sticky honeydew on which sooty mould grows. They are dangerous as vectors: they carry viruses from sick plants to healthy ones as they feed (whiteflies spread cassava mosaic disease).

Boring insects have larvae (or adults) that bore into stems, fruits and seeds. Examples: stem borers in maize and sugar cane, maize weevils, bean weevils, cowpea beetles. Damage: hidden, because the harm is inside; plants wilt and die and stored grain is hollowed out.

img.alt: A stem borer larva inside a damaged maize stem

p: Nematodes (eelworms) are tiny worms in the soil. Root-knot nematodes make swellings (galls) on roots, so the plant cannot take in water and minerals and becomes stunted and wilts.

Birds, such as quelea and weaver birds, eat ripening cereals (millet, sorghum, rice). Rodents (rats, squirrels, cane rats) gnaw stems and eat stored grain and tubers. Others: monkeys, snails and slugs.

Lower yield and lower quality, so the farmer earns less. Higher cost of production (chemicals and labour). Heavy losses in stores (post-harvest losses), leading to food shortage. Total crop failure in bad outbreaks (locust swarms, fall armyworm). Contamination of food with droppings and with poisons made by moulds. Fall armyworm, first found in Nigeria in 2016, has reduced the yields of maize across many states.

title: Diseases of Crops
summary: Fungal, bacterial and viral crop diseases, their symptoms, how they spread and the causal agent of each.

p: A disease is any change from the normal growth and working of a plant, caused by a pathogen (a germ) or by something in the environment (such as lack of a mineral). Most are caused by fungi, bacteria and viruses.

img.alt: A chart of crop diseases showing symptoms on cocoa pods, maize and cassava leaves
img.cap: Some crop diseases and their symptoms.

p: Fungi are the most common cause of plant disease. They spread by spores carried by wind, water splash, insects and soil.

Black pod of cocoa: black patches rot the pods and the beans. Maize smut: large black swellings (galls) full of powdery spores on the cobs, tassels or stalks. Rusts: orange, red or brown powdery spots on leaves (maize rust). Mildews: white, powdery or downy growth on leaf surfaces. Others: anthracnose and leaf spots on many crops.

Spread by splashes of rain, by tools, by insects and by infected planting material. Examples: Cassava bacterial blight (angular leaf spots, wilting and dying back of shoots); citrus canker (raised corky spots on fruits, leaves and stems); bacterial wilt of tomato and pepper.

Viruses are carried by vectors, mainly sap-sucking insects such as aphids and whiteflies, and by cuttings taken from sick plants. Examples: Cassava mosaic disease (yellow and green mosaic on leaves, small twisted leaves and a big loss of yield); Maize streak virus (yellow streaks along the veins, stunted plants; carried by leafhoppers); groundnut rosette (carried by aphids); cocoa swollen shoot (carried by mealybugs).
Viruses cannot be cured with sprays. We can only prevent them, by killing the vectors, removing sick plants and planting resistant varieties.
Maize smut: fungus. Citrus canker: bacterium. Cassava mosaic disease: virus. Black pod: fungus (Phytophthora, an oomycete often grouped with fungi). Cassava bacterial blight: bacterium.

Reduced yield and quality; money lost on chemicals; failure of whole crops in an epidemic; and mycotoxins (poisons made by some fungi, such as aflatoxin in groundnuts and maize) that can harm people and animals.

title: Control of Pests and Diseases
summary: Cultural, biological, chemical, physical, legal and genetic control, and the idea of integrated pest management.

p: There is no single best way. Farmers combine several, which is called integrated pest management (IPM).

img.alt: A diagram of integrated pest management with cultural, biological, chemical and physical control around a crop

p: Cultural control (changing the way we farm): crop rotation (pests of one crop starve when another is planted); field sanitation (removing and destroying crop remains and weeds that hide pests; burying or composting is better than burning, because open burning pollutes the air); using clean seeds and healthy planting materials; correct spacing for air flow, which lowers the humidity that fungi like; early or late planting to avoid the pest peak; clean weeding.

Biological control (using natural enemies): ladybirds eat aphids; the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) kills certain caterpillars but is harmless to people; parasitic wasps lay eggs in pests; encouraging insect-eating birds. It is safe and long-lasting, but slow and works only for some pests.

Chemical control (pesticides): insecticides for insects, fungicides for fungi, nematicides for nematodes, rodenticides for rodents, herbicides for weeds. It is fast and effective, but it is expensive, can pollute soil and water, can kill useful insects such as bees, and pests can become resistant. Always follow the label, wear protective clothing and keep chemicals away from children and food.
Physical or mechanical control: hand-picking caterpillars; traps (light, sticky and pheromone traps); nets and scarecrows against birds; drying and proper storage of grain; flooding or heating soil.
Legal (quarantine) control: laws and inspection at borders to stop foreign pests and diseases from being brought in on seeds and plants.
Genetic control (plant breeding): breeding resistant varieties, such as cassava resistant to mosaic disease (the TME varieties) and insect-resistant cowpea.

Biological: advantage, safe for the environment and long-lasting; disadvantage, slow and may not completely remove the pest. Chemical: advantage, fast and effective; disadvantage, harmful to the environment and non-target organisms, and pests may become resistant.
